messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 27
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Physical Therapist
- Trauma Type: Sexual assault
- Pcl5: 49

**Patient Vignette: "Amir" (Age 27, Male, Physical Therapist)**

Amir comes to session dressed in a clean, pressed polo shirt and khakis, his posture rigidly upright. He offers a brief, controlled smile before sitting on the edge of the chair, hands resting on his knees. He is a physical therapist at a busy outpatient clinic, a job he once loved for its clarity and purpose. Now, it feels like a daily minefield.

The trauma happened fourteen months ago, at a professional conference for sports medicine. Amir had been a rising star in his field, invited to present a workshop on manual therapy techniques. The second evening, he went for a drink with a group of colleagues. One of them, a senior therapist he had admired and trusted, offered to walk him back to his hotel. Amir remembers the hallway lights, the key card in his hand, the sudden shift in the other man’s demeanor. He remembers being pushed inside his own room, the door clicking shut. He remembers the weight, the smell of stale beer and expensive cologne, the feeling of his wrists pinned to the pillow. He did not fight back. He froze. He remembers thinking, very clearly, *If I just stay still, it will be over.* It was.

Afterward, Amir showered for forty-five minutes. He did not call the police. He did not tell his wife, Leila. He told himself it was a mistake, a bizarre lapse in judgment, something he could just erase. He flew home the next day and went back to work on Monday.

The erasure did not work. Within weeks, Amir began to feel a low, constant hum of dread in the clinic. He started avoiding the treatment rooms with the heavy, locking doors. He began scheduling his appointments in the open gym area, even when it was inappropriate for the patient’s condition. When a male patient would reach out to grab his hand for support during an exercise, Amir would flinch, a sharp, involuntary jerk that he would try to cover with a cough. He stopped using the manual therapy techniques he was known for—the deep, sustained pressure on a muscle belly—because the sensation of his hands on a prone, trusting body made his stomach turn. He started assigning those patients to his colleagues, making excuses about his “wrist acting up.”

At home, he has become quiet. Leila has noticed he no longer wants to be the big spoon. He sleeps on the very edge of the bed, facing the door. He has not initiated sex in over a year. When she reaches for him in the dark, he goes rigid, his heart hammering so loud he is sure she can hear it. He says he’s just tired. He is tired. He wakes up at 3:17 AM every single night, drenched in a cold sweat, the smell of that cologne in his nostrils. He spends the hour before dawn scrolling through workout videos on his phone, anything to drown out the replay of the lock clicking shut.

The worst part, he says, is the shame. He is a man. He is a physical therapist, a healer of bodies. He is supposed to be strong, in control. He feels like a fraud. He looks at his wife and sees a stranger, because he is keeping a secret so large it has hollowed him out. He feels a profound, aching loneliness. He cannot tell anyone, because if he does, he will have to admit that he did not fight back. That he just lay there. And that, to him, feels like a worse violation than the one he endured.
